drills.q: Name the frontend XSS sinks that matter in a modern codebase, and explain why React's default rendering avoids the most common class.
drills.a: innerHTML/outerHTML, dangerouslySetInnerHTML, eval/new Function, document.write, javascript: URLs, string-arg setTimeout/setInterval. React JSX {value} interpolation auto-escapes by default, so the vulnerability requires deliberately opting into dangerouslySetInnerHTML rather than being the default behavior.

drills.q: If a feature genuinely needs to render user-supplied HTML (rich text), what's the correct approach, and why not a hand-rolled regex sanitizer?
drills.a: Sanitize with a library like DOMPurify using an explicit allowlist of tags/attributes before passing to dangerouslySetInnerHTML. Regex can't reliably parse HTML and is a well-documented source of sanitizer bypasses -- avoidance isn't an option since the feature requirement is real.

drills.q: Why is nonce-based CSP with strict-dynamic preferred over host-allowlist CSP, and what single mistake completely defeats a nonce-based policy?
drills.a: Host allowlists break constantly since third-party scripts load further scripts from unanticipated origins, and any allowlisted domain with an open redirect becomes a bypass. strict-dynamic propagates trust cryptographically instead. A static or reused nonce (not freshly random per HTTP response) completely defeats the mechanism.

drills.q: Explain precisely what CORS protects against, and correct the misconception that a CORS error means the request never reached the server.
drills.a: CORS is a browser-enforced restriction on JS reading a cross-origin response, not a server-side authorization mechanism -- it doesn't stop the request from being sent or processed. A CORS error in the console typically means the request DID reach the server and already had its side effects (e.g. a DB write on POST); the browser just blocked the script from reading the response.

drills.q: Why is dynamically reflecting the Origin header as Access-Control-Allow-Origin dangerous, and how do you correctly support multiple legitimate credentialed origins?
drills.a: It reintroduces the same vulnerability the spec's block on '*' + credentials:true prevents -- any origin can make a credentialed request and read the response -- while looking compliant since it's not the literal wildcard. Correct approach: validate the incoming Origin against an explicit server-side allowlist and only echo it back when it matches.

drills.q: Compare localStorage, HttpOnly cookie, and in-memory token storage, and state the 2026 practitioner consensus.
drills.a: localStorage: readable by any XSS, full silent account takeover risk. HttpOnly cookie: invisible to JS (immune to XSS read) but auto-sent by browser, introducing CSRF surface. In-memory: minimizes exposure window (nothing persisted) but needs a working silent-refresh flow. Consensus: short-lived access token in memory + refresh token in HttpOnly+Secure+SameSite cookie + CSRF token on state-changing endpoints.

drills.q: Explain clickjacking mechanically and the current correct defense, including a common implementation mistake.
drills.a: An attacker embeds the target in an invisible/positioned iframe, overlays decoy UI, tricking clicks on a hidden real button underneath. Defense: Content-Security-Policy: frame-ancestors 'self' (or explicit allowlist), which wins over legacy X-Frame-Options in CSP2+ browsers. Common mistake: setting X-Frame-Options via a <meta> tag, which has no effect -- it only works as a real HTTP response header.

drills.q: Describe the September 2025 npm supply-chain incident (chalk/debug/Shai-Hulud) and what it structurally demonstrates about dependency risk.
drills.a: A phishing attack against one npm maintainer compromised 18 packages (chalk, debug, ansi-styles, strip-ansi -- 2.6B combined weekly downloads) with a crypto-wallet-targeting payload, followed by the self-propagating Shai-Hulud worm (500+ packages wave 1, tens of thousands of repos by a November 2025 '2.0' campaign). It demonstrates the vulnerability lived in a transitive dependency several layers removed from any affected team's own code -- direct usage isn't required for exposure.

drills.q: Design CSRF protection for a system that just moved auth tokens from localStorage to HttpOnly cookies, and explain why SameSite alone isn't sufficient.
drills.a: Set SameSite=Lax/Strict as a first layer, then add an explicit CSRF token on state-changing endpoints -- either the synchronizer token pattern (server-issued token embedded in page, validated on submit) or double-submit cookie (a second non-HttpOnly cookie the client must echo as a header, unreadable cross-origin). SameSite=Lax still allows top-level GET navigations to carry the cookie, and browser enforcement nuances mean it's a strong mitigation, not a complete guarantee.

drills.q: A team's own application code never directly imports a package later found compromised in a supply-chain attack. Were they still at risk, and what are the practical mitigations regardless of direct usage?
drills.a: Yes -- if the compromised package was anywhere in the transitive dependency tree, it still executes in the same process/build environment with the same permissions; direct usage isn't required for exposure. Mitigations: commit and enforce lockfiles to prevent silent version drift on install, run supply-chain-specific scanning in CI (behavioral analysis like Socket/Snyk, not just CVE matching), minimize dependency surface, and apply extra scrutiny to auto-merge bots on auth/crypto/build-tooling dependencies.
